questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Coils of lead were laid in earthenware pots over vinegar, the pots were buried in spent tanning bark, and the stack was left for three months while the heat of the rotting bark drove the reaction. What came out was a dense white carbonate that covered better than any other pigment then available. Painters accepted a material slow to make and dangerous to grind because nothing else was so _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A navigator trained in the Caroline Islands holds a course by the point on the horizon at which a known star rises or sets, changing star as each one climbs too high to be of use. The canoe is treated as still, with the sea and the islands moving past it, and progress is tracked by counting off the changing bearing of an island that lies out of sight to one side. The whole reckoning is kept _____.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “body” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A thrower judges a clay by how far it will stand up before it slumps. Ball clay is plastic and takes a shape easily but shrinks and warps in the kiln; coarse sand worked into it stiffens the mixture at the cost of some of that ease. The <u>body</u> a workshop settles on is always a compromise between what the wheel wants and what the fire will allow.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A prepared mixture of clay from which ware is made.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The physical structure of a person or an animal.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The main part of a written work.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A group of people acting together as a unit.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “run” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The compositor's work is over once the forme is locked up, and from that point the cost of a book falls almost entirely on paper and press time. Setting the type a second time would cost what the first setting cost; pulling more sheets while the type is still standing costs little beyond the paper. A publisher therefore fixes the size of the <u>run</u> before the first sheet is pulled.

choices.label: A
choices.content: An enclosure in which animals are kept.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A continuous period of a particular condition.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The number of copies printed at one time.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A journey made regularly by a vehicle.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Lead on its own casts a letter with soft corners, and the shoulders of the type crumble after a few thousand impressions. Tin and antimony added to the melt give an alloy that expands very slightly as it sets, so the metal is pressed into every angle of the mould instead of shrinking away from it. A founder chooses the mixture for the _____ of the face it produces rather than for the strength of the bar it casts.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A vatman making paper by hand dips a mould, shakes it until the fibres lock, and couches off a single sheet; a good pair might manage a thousand a day between them. <u>The machine patented for the Fourdrinier brothers ran the pulp onto an endless belt of woven wire, so that a sheet was never formed at all but cut out of a continuous web.</u> Deckle edges disappeared, sheet sizes became arbitrary, and the length of a sheet ceased to be set by the reach of a man's arms.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It explains why printers continued to prefer handmade paper.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It reports the daily output a pair of hand papermakers could manage.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It questions whether the brothers deserve the credit for the design.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It identifies the change in method whose consequences the rest of the text sets out.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Beetle larvae in a wooden frame can be killed with a fumigant, but residues stay in the object and reach the conservator who handles it afterwards. <u>Sealing the frame in a barrier bag and flushing it with nitrogen until the oxygen falls below half a per cent kills the larvae and leaves nothing behind.</u> The treatment takes three weeks rather than an afternoon, and the frame comes out of the bag chemically as it went in.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It describes the residues that a fumigant leaves in an object.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It presents the alternative whose advantage the rest of the text explains.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It concedes that the treatment frequently fails to kill the larvae.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It explains why beetle larvae attack wooden frames in the first place.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: On the plain around Lake Titicaca, fields were built up into long platforms with water-filled channels dug between them. A ridge raised in this way sits above the cold air that pools on the plain at night, and the water in the channels gives back through the small hours the heat it took up during the day. Trial plots rebuilt on the old pattern in the 1980s came through frosts that killed the crop in flat fields alongside them.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The platforms were built to bring the crop within easier reach of harvesters.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The raised-field layout shields a crop from frost, and rebuilt plots have shown the effect directly.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The channels between the platforms were dug chiefly to irrigate the crop in dry months.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Flat fields around the lake yield more than raised ones in most years.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Common earthenware fires to a buff or a red that no transparent glaze will hide. Tin oxide stirred into a lead glaze makes it opaque and white, so a cheap clay leaves the kiln looking like something else, and the painter works on a white ground with much of the freedom a porcelain decorator has. The glaze is unforgiving in one respect: a brushstroke sinks into the raw powdery surface at once and cannot be lifted off again.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Tin-glazed earthenware is fired at a higher temperature than porcelain is.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Painters preferred earthenware to porcelain because of its warmer colour.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The opacity of the glaze comes from the lead in it rather than from the tin.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The tin glaze gives a common clay a white surface to paint on, at the cost of allowing no correction.

questions.stem: Which quotation from the diary most effectively illustrates Lindqvist's claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A member of a 1911 Antarctic party kept a diary through the season of depot-laying that preceded the main journey. Historian Sofia Lindqvist argues that the diary treats the placing of the supply depots, rather than the journey they were meant to support, as the work on which everything turned.

choices.label: A
choices.content: “The ponies took their feed badly and one is lame in the near fore.”

choices.label: B
choices.content: “We are eleven miles short of where the depot should stand, and every mile we fail to carry now is a mile the party must carry in the spring, when it can least afford to.”

choices.label: C
choices.content: “Read aloud in the tent for an hour after the evening meal.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “The wind dropped towards evening and the light on the barrier was very fine.”

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
A port authority compared four quays over a single year, recording the cargo handled at each and the average time a ship spent alongside it.
QuayCargo handled (thousand tonnes)Average time alongside (hours)
North Quay41031
East Jetty39019
Old Basin24044
Ferry Quay15512
The authority argued that tonnage on its own is a poor measure of how hard a quay is worked, pointing out that the quay handling the most cargo was not the quickest to turn a ship round: _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: Old Basin handled 240 thousand tonnes and held a ship alongside for 44 hours.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Ferry Quay turned a ship round in 12 hours, the shortest average time recorded.

choices.label: C
choices.content: East Jetty handled 390 thousand tonnes, the second largest figure in the table.

choices.label: D
choices.content: North Quay handled 410 thousand tonnes but held a ship 31 hours on average, while East Jetty handled 390 thousand tonnes in 19 hours.

questions.stem: Which quotation from the notebook most effectively illustrates Vandenberg's claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A conservator who treated a group of painted panels in the 1950s kept a working notebook alongside the formal treatment records. Curator Piet Vandenberg argues that the notebook shows her subordinating the appearance of a finished panel to the requirement that anything she added could later be taken off again.

choices.label: A
choices.content: “Chose the weaker adhesive for the flaking edge although the stronger holds better, since the stronger cannot be got off again without the paint.”

choices.label: B
choices.content: “The losses along the lower edge are numerous but small.”

choices.label: C
choices.content: “Worked four days on the sky, which is the part a visitor sees first.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “The panel was photographed under raking light before any work began.”

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Paper ground from wood carries acids left in the sheet when it was made, and those acids go on cutting the cellulose chains for as long as they remain there. Washing a sheet in an alkaline solution leaves a small reserve in the fibre that neutralises acid as it is produced. The treatment cannot give back the strength a brittle sheet has already lost, which means its value lies in _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: identifying the mill at which the paper was made.

choices.label: B
choices.content: slowing the damage still to come rather than repairing the damage already done.

choices.label: C
choices.content: returning the sheet to the strength it had when it was new.

choices.label: D
choices.content: removing the printed image so that the fibre can be used again.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Glass cools from the outside inward, and the surface that sets first is put under strain as the interior contracts behind it. A vessel taken straight from the blowing iron into the open air may hold enough of that strain to fly apart days later without being touched. Passing it slowly down a heated tunnel lets the whole thickness come down together, which means that the tunnel's purpose is to _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: shape the vessel after it has left the blowing iron.

choices.label: B
choices.content: even out the rate at which different parts of the glass cool.

choices.label: C
choices.content: raise the glass to a temperature higher than the furnace reached.

choices.label: D
choices.content: harden the surface of the glass against scratching.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A mason bee lives alone and makes no honey. Each female stocks a row of cells in a hollow stem with pollen and seals them off with _____ garden wall fitted with bundles of cut stems will hold hundreds of them by the second season.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A mushroom flicks its spores sideways into the still air between the gills, and it does so with no moving part at all. The mechanism needs three _____ a drop of water condensed at the base of the spore, a film of water spread over the spore's surface, and the sudden merging of the two.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Depths on a chart are reckoned from a level chosen so that the tide will very seldom fall below it. The figure printed beside a shoal is therefore not the depth a ship will find _____ is the depth it can count on finding at almost any state of the tide.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A plaster mould draws water out of the liquid clay poured into it, so a skin thickens against the wall while the middle stays fluid. The caster tips the surplus back out after a few _____ of even thickness is left standing in the mould.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Beekeepers who open a hive in cold weather do more harm than good, and a colony chilled in March may never build up. The inspector, together with the two volunteers who hold the frames, _____ to work quickly once the crown board is off.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The harbour's dues books run back to 1840, but the volumes covering the war years were never bound and have come apart into loose sheets. Neither the archivist nor the two volunteers sorting them _____ willing to guess at the order the sheets once stood in.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The kiln is drawn on a Friday, and every piece is checked against the firing book before it is packed. When the crate reached Bristol and the dealer's men lifted the straw out of it, they found that three of the plates _____ somewhere between the bench and the carrier's cart.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Glassmakers around the Mediterranean used soda from mineral sources and from the ash of coastal plants, and their glass has lain two thousand years in the ground with little change. _____ the forest glasshouses of northern Europe used potash from burnt beech, and their windows weather into a crust that eats the surface away.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A breakwater faced with rough quarry stone loses blocks in the first heavy winter, because a rounded boulder rolls once the sea has undercut it. _____ modern breakwaters are armoured with cast concrete shapes whose limbs hook into their neighbours and which lock tighter as the sea works on them.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Before the deep-water docks were cut, a ship too big for the quay lay at anchor in the river and her cargo was carried ashore in barges. Every ton was handled twice and paid for twice. _____ a port that could bring a ship alongside undercut its neighbours long before it could load one any faster.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the finisher's judgement of the tool's heat matters so much. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A finisher decorates a leather binding by pressing heated brass tools into the leather.
  • Gold leaf is laid over an adhesive of egg white and vinegar called glaire.
  • The tool must be hot enough to fix the leaf but not so hot that it scorches the leather.
  • A finisher judges the heat by touching the tool to a damp sponge and listening to it.
  • An impression made at the wrong heat cannot be removed and the cover is spoiled.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Gold leaf is laid over an adhesive of egg white and vinegar called glaire.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Because an impression made at the wrong heat cannot be removed, the finisher tests the tool by ear against a damp sponge before it ever touches the cover.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A finisher judges the heat by touching the tool to a damp sponge and listening to it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A finisher decorates a leather binding by pressing heated brass tools into the leather.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why some of the tombs have survived intact. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Chachapoya buried some of their dead in tombs built into cliff faces in northern Peru.
  • At Revash the tombs stand out from the ledges as small houses with painted walls.
  • The ledges can be reached only from above, by rope.
  • Looting has emptied many of the tombs that are easier to reach.
  • Tombs on the least accessible ledges have been found with their contents undisturbed.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The Chachapoya buried some of their dead in tombs built into cliff faces in northern Peru.

choices.label: B
choices.content: At Revash the tombs stand out from the ledges as small houses with painted walls.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Looting has emptied many of the tombs that are easier to reach.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Because the least accessible ledges can be reached only from above by rope, the tombs standing on them have been found with their contents undisturbed.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain what the 1976 passage was intended to demonstrate. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Hōkūle‘a is a double-hulled canoe launched in Hawaii in 1975.
  • It was built to test whether long Pacific passages could be sailed without instruments.
  • Its 1976 passage to Tahiti was navigated by Mau Piailug of Satawal.
  • No compass, chart or clock was carried on that passage.
  • Piailug afterwards taught the method to Hawaiian navigators.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Hōkūle‘a is a double-hulled canoe launched in Hawaii in 1975.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Sailed to Tahiti in 1976 with no compass, chart or clock aboard, the canoe was meant to show that a long Pacific passage could be navigated without instruments.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Mau Piailug of Satawal navigated the passage and afterwards taught the method to Hawaiian navigators.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The canoe was launched in Hawaii in 1975 and reached Tahiti the following year.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Iron gall ink is made by steeping crushed oak galls in water and adding green vitriol, and the black it produces bites into the fibre of the page rather than resting on top of it. A scribe's error could not be brushed away; it had to be scraped off with a knife, taking a layer of the parchment with it. What made the ink so useful to a chancery is exactly what made it _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Ordinary lime mortar sets by drying and will not harden at all under water, which is why the first towers on the Eddystone reef were built of timber and were washed away. Burning limestones from one quarry after another, John Smeaton found that those containing clay set hard while submerged. The mortar he settled on was _____ in the one condition that had defeated everything used before it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A lichen colonising bare rock spreads outward at a rate that varies little from year to year on a given site, so the largest disc on a boulder gives a minimum age for the surface beneath it. Where a glacier has left a moraine that no document records and no wood survives to be dated, measuring the discs supplies a figure that would otherwise be _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A sheet lifted from the vat is a mat of felted fibre that drinks up whatever is written on it, so a line of ink spreads outward until the letter is a blot. Papermakers therefore dip the dried sheet in a bath of gelatine, which fills the spaces between the fibres and leaves a surface the ink can sit on. Sizing does not alter the fibre; it alters how _____ the sheet is.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Add the ash of calcined bone to a porcelain body and the fired result passes light where a stoneware cup would not, yet it chips less readily than the hard-paste porcelains made on the continent. English factories took up the recipe because a crate of it survived carriage and still looked like porcelain on the table. The material's appeal lay in being at once translucent and _____.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A flight of locks lifts a boat up a hillside by filling and emptying chambers, and every passage sends a lockful of water down to the level below. <u>An inclined plane instead carries the boat itself, afloat in a tank that runs up a slope on rails, with the two tanks counterweighted against each other.</u> Water is spent only in topping up the tanks, and a boat that would have taken half a day in a staircase of chambers reaches the summit in twenty minutes.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It describes the arrangement whose advantages the final sentence reports.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It explains why locks came to be built in flights rather than singly.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It concedes a drawback of the inclined plane that was never overcome.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It gives the cost of building an inclined plane.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A male lyrebird's song is largely other birds' songs. Recordings from one Victorian population carry the calls of a dozen species, delivered in sequence and with the timing of the originals. Young males copy from older males rather than from the species themselves, so a phrase can persist in a lyrebird population long after the bird that supplied it has left the district. The song is in that sense a record of what was once heard there, kept by birds that never heard it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It presents two rival accounts of the song and endorses one of them.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It traces the spread of a species from one region into another.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It lists the imitated species in order of how often they occur.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It states a general claim, gives evidence for it, and draws out a consequence of the way the songs are learned.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A varroa mite feeds on a developing bee inside its cell and on the adult that emerges from it. Colonies collapse with far more damage than the feeding alone accounts for: the wound is a doorway, and viruses that sit at low levels in untroubled colonies multiply once a mite is carrying them from bee to bee. A beekeeper counting mites on a sticky board is watching a vector rather than a parasite.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Viruses are absent from colonies in which no mites are found.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Counting mites tells a beekeeper very little about the health of a colony.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Much of the harm the mite does comes from the viruses it transmits rather than from its feeding.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The mite feeds on adult bees only and not on developing ones.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Potatoes spread on the ground of the high plateau freeze through the night and thaw in the day's sun, and the villagers tread them to press out the water that the freezing has driven from the cells. Repeated over several days, the tubers become light, hard and pale, and they keep for years in a dry store. The alternation of hard frost and strong sun belongs to the altitude, so the food is a product of the plateau rather than something carried up onto it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The process requires a fire to dry the tubers at the end.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Villagers took the technique from neighbours in the lowlands.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The method of preservation depends on conditions particular to the high plateau.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The treated tubers keep for a single season and no longer.

questions.stem: Which quotation from the report most effectively illustrates Kerrigan's claim?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: In 1868 the engineer to a small tidal harbour submitted a report on a proposed extension of the north pier. Historian Ada Kerrigan argues that the report's real object was to warn the trustees that the harbour's difficulty lay in the annual cost of keeping its channel open, and not in the length of its pier.

choices.label: A
choices.content: “The extension would carry the pier head some ninety feet further into deep water.”

choices.label: B
choices.content: “The masonry of the existing pier was examined and found sound throughout its length.”

choices.label: C
choices.content: “Vessels of the coasting trade have increased in number since the last survey was made.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “Whatever is built, the sand returns each winter, and the sum laid out in clearing it has for eleven years together exceeded the sum laid out in building.”

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
Honey sealed under a wax capping keeps indefinitely, while honey left uncapped takes up water from the air and may ferment; fermentation becomes likely above about twenty per cent water. A beekeeper recorded the water content of honey drawn from sealed and from unsealed comb at four apiaries in the same season.
ApiaryWater content, sealed comb (%)Water content, unsealed comb (%)
Ashgrove17.220.9
Braemore16.821.4
Cairnhead17.619.8
Dunmore17.122.3
The unsealed honey passed twenty per cent at three of the four apiaries, and the widest difference between sealed and unsealed honey was recorded at _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: Ashgrove, where the unsealed comb held 20.9 per cent water.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Dunmore, where 22.3 per cent in the unsealed comb stood against 17.1 per cent in the sealed comb.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Cairnhead, where the unsealed comb held 19.8 per cent water.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Braemore, where the sealed comb held the least water of any apiary.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ostrander's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Households in some Andean valleys held plots at several altitudes at once, from maize land low down to herding ground on the high grassland. Archaeologist Neil Ostrander argues that the arrangement was a deliberate way of drawing on several climates at once, rather than a consequence of population pressure pushing families onto marginal land.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Households holding high and low plots together were among the largest and best provided in their communities, and the outlying plots were taken up in years when land on the valley floor was still unclaimed.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Journeys between the highest and the lowest plots took several days on foot.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Maize was grown only below a certain altitude.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Some communities held plots on both slopes of the same valley.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A crab-claw sail is a triangle held between two spars with its point at the foot, and it drives a hull well with the wind on the beam or behind. Voyaging canoes carrying it could not be pushed far into a headwind, and the sailing directions preserved in the islands describe waiting out a season rather than beating against it. It follows that the timing of a voyage in such a canoe was _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: determined chiefly by the length of the hull.

choices.label: B
choices.content: settled by the number of paddlers who could be found.

choices.label: C
choices.content: governed by the prevailing wind rather than chosen freely.

choices.label: D
choices.content: unaffected by the direction from which the wind blew.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Snow returns most of the ultraviolet light falling on it, so a traveller on an ice sheet takes it from below as well as from above, and an overcast day gives little protection because cloud scatters the light without absorbing much of it. The injury it causes appears some hours after the exposure that produced it. A party that has spent a grey day on the ice without eye protection will therefore _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: have been shielded from harm by the cloud cover.

choices.label: B
choices.content: notice the injury within the first minutes of exposure.

choices.label: C
choices.content: have received ultraviolet light only from directly overhead.

choices.label: D
choices.content: not know until the evening how much damage the day has done.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A pony breaks through crust that a dog runs over, and it cannot be fed on what a sledging party is already hauling for itself. Roald Amundsen, an experienced traveller in the Canadian _____ dogs from the outset and planned to kill the weaker ones as the loads went down.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

questions.stem: The student wants to explain the difficulty a painter faced in working with smalt. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Smalt is powdered blue glass coloured with cobalt.
  • It was the cheapest strong blue available to painters in the sixteenth century.
  • The colour is strong only while the particles are coarse; ground finer, smalt turns pale.
  • Coarse particles are hard to disperse in oil and leave a gritty paint.
  • Potassium leaches out of the glass over time and many smalt passages have turned grey.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Smalt was the cheapest strong blue available to painters in the sixteenth century.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Smalt is powdered blue glass coloured with cobalt.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A painter had to choose between a strong blue in coarse particles that left the paint gritty and a smoother paint that finer grinding had made pale.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Potassium leaches out of the glass over time, and many smalt passages have turned grey.

  • The gates can be opened only while the water outside stands level with the water inside.
  • At Liverpool a half-tide basin was built in front of the wet dock.
  • The basin lengthened the period each day during which ships could pass in and out.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Because a wet dock's gates open only at level water, an intermediate basin was built in front of it to lengthen the period each day during which ships could pass.

choices.label: B
choices.content: At Liverpool a half-tide basin was built in front of the wet dock.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A tidal harbour empties as the tide falls, and the ships in it take the ground twice a day.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The gates of a wet dock can be opened only while the water outside stands level with the water inside.

choices.content: The trough is made of cast-iron plates bolted together and bedded in Welsh flannel and lead.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

questions.passage: A chip log is a weighted board on a line knotted at even intervals. Thrown over the stern, the board stays roughly where it entered the water while the ship draws line off a reel, and a hand counts the knots that pass through his fingers while a small sand glass empties. Speed is read off directly in knots, because the spacing of the knots and the running time of the glass are chosen to make the count come out in sea miles an hour. questions.passage: A young zebra finch raised where it can hear an adult male copies that bird's song, and by about ninety days its own song has stopped changing. Playing a tutor's song to such a bird after the period has closed changes very little.

choices.content: Brown-rot fungi are more common in conifer timber than in hardwoods.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nowicka's argument?

questions.passage: Male white-crowned sparrows in adjoining valleys sing recognisably different versions of the species song, and the boundary between the two versions falls in the same place from year to year. choices.content: The two versions of the song differ mainly in the length of the opening whistle.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The boundary follows a ridge that the birds seldom cross in winter.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Males respond more strongly to playback of their own valley's version than to the neighbouring one.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Males ringed as nestlings in one valley and later found breeding in the other sing the version of the valley they settled in, and pairings across the boundary are as frequent as pairings within it.

Supers on the hiveNumber of hives
14
27
39
45
What is the median number of supers per hive in this apiary?

questions.stem: A lighthouse keeper's short ladder leans against the tower with its foot 2.8 metres from the wall and its top 9.6 metres up the wall. A long ladder leans against the same wall at the same angle, with its top 24 metres up the wall. How many metres from the wall is the foot of the long ladder?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A hawser is made fast to a bollard on a level quay and runs straight up to a fitting on a mast, making an angle of 60° with the quay. The bollard is 14 metres from the foot of the mast. How many metres of hawser run from the bollard to the fitting?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A rope walk's curing tank is a rectangular box measuring 3 metres by 1.2 metres by 0.8 metres. Tar is pumped into the empty tank at 96 litres per minute, and one cubic metre is 1,000 litres. How many minutes does the tank take to fill?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A glassworks makes two funnels of the same shape, one a scaled copy of the other. The smaller funnel stands 12 centimetres tall and holds 96 cubic centimetres. The larger funnel stands 18 centimetres tall. How many cubic centimetres does the larger funnel hold?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A bottle works packs 12 bottles into each crate and packed 336 bottles in one morning. How many crates did the works pack that morning?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A printing house charges $19 to make up the plates for a poster and then $6 for each poster printed. An order came to $97 in all. How many posters were printed?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A pilot boat charges a $30 call-out plus $45 for each hour it is at sea. What is the total charge, in dollars, for a job lasting 4 hours?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A warp beam is wound with 1,200 metres of thread, and 15 metres are woven off it each hour the loom runs. Which expression gives the number of metres of thread left on the beam after the loom has run for h hours?

questions.stem: A bee inspector must visit at least 15 apiaries this month. Which inequality gives all the possible numbers a of apiaries the inspector may visit this month?

questions.stem: A dock gauge reports the height of the water as H=1.8+0.6t, where H is the height in metres and t is the number of hours after low water. What does 1.8 represent in this model?

choices.label: B
choices.content: The number of metres by which the height rises each hour.

questions.stem: A ferry company charges freight by the tonne, at one rate for salt and another rate for glass sand. Carrying 5 tonnes of salt together with 2 tonnes of glass sand costs $94, and carrying 2 tonnes of salt together with 5 tonnes of glass sand costs $109. What does it cost to carry 1 tonne of salt together with 1 tonne of glass sand?
questions.subject: MATH

Reading xCorrection \(f(x)\)
3-2
1114
What is the value of \(f(0)\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A freight ferry may carry a total of at most 4,200 kilograms on its cargo deck. Each pallet of glass weighs 180 kilograms and each pallet of salt weighs 120 kilograms, and the operator requires at least twice as many salt pallets as glass pallets on every sailing. On a sailing carrying exactly 9 pallets of glass, what is the greatest number of pallets of salt the ferry can carry?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem:
A stowage calculation uses the system
3x+2y=17
5x-4y=k
where x and y are the numbers of tonnes of two cargoes and k is a constant. The solution of this system has y=4. What is the value of k?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A ferry company sets the fare for a crossing of d nautical miles as F=a+bd dollars, where a and b are constants. A crossing of 12 nautical miles costs $39 and a crossing of 20 nautical miles costs $59. Which expression gives F in terms of d?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A glassworks must turn out at least 500 bottles in a day. Its older machine turns out 40 bottles an hour and its newer machine turns out 65 bottles an hour, and the two machines run independently of each other. If the older machine runs for a hours and the newer machine runs for b hours, which inequality must hold if the day's target is met?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A printing house bought 3 reams of laid paper and 4 reams of wove paper for $131, and on another day bought 5 reams of laid paper and 2 reams of wove paper for $139. How many dollars more does one ream of laid paper cost than one ream of wove paper?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A dyeing line puts every skein through two stages. The first stage converts a raw reading x into \(g(x)=\frac{x}{2}+3\), and the second stage converts a value u coming out of the first stage into \(f(u)=u^{2}-4u\). Which expression gives \(f(g(x))\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A glassworks writes the difference of two cooling rates as \(\frac{2}{x-3}-\frac{1}{x+2}\), where \(x>3\). Which expression is equivalent to that difference?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: Setting a press's feed reduces to the equation \(\frac{6}{x-2}=x+3\), where \(x\ne 2\). What is the sum of all the solutions of this equation?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A glass furnace's temperature deviation is modelled by \(d(x)=a(x-6)^{2}-40\), where x is the number of hours since firing began, a is a positive constant, and d is measured in degrees Celsius. The model gives \(d(2)=8\). What is the value of \(d(9)\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: At a rope walk, one tarring machine can coat a whole batch of rope in 6 hours and a second machine can coat the same batch in 12 hours. If both machines work on one batch at the same time, each at its own steady rate, how many hours does the batch take?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A glassworks drew 200 bottles at random from one day's output of 15,000 bottles and found 6 of the 200 to be flawed. Based on this sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of flawed bottles in that day's output?

questions.stem: A quay holds 12 bales of raw wool whose mean mass is 84 kilograms. One bale is carted away, and the mean mass of the 11 bales left behind is 82 kilograms. What is the mass, in kilograms, of the bale that was carted away?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A bottle works cut the number of bottles it rejects by 25% in one year and then cut the reduced number by a further 20% in the next year. It rejected 240 bottles in the second of those years. How many bottles did it reject in the year before either cut?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A solid glass float in the shape of a sphere of radius 6 centimetres is melted down and recast, with none of the glass lost, as a solid cylinder 18 centimetres tall. What is the radius, in centimetres, of the cylinder?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A sailmaker lofts a triangular staysail \(ABC\) in which the angle at A measures twice the angle at B. The side \(AC\) is extended beyond C, and the angle between that extension and the side \(BC\) measures 129°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the angle at B?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A drawing office sets out a right triangle \(PQR\) with its right angle at Q, so \(PR\) is the longest side. The office records \(\sin R=\frac{8}{17}\) and \(PR=51\). What is the length of \(QR\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A tide mill's grain hopper is a rectangular box whose length is twice its width and whose height is 3 metres. The hopper holds 150 cubic metres. What is the width, in metres, of the hopper?
